name: AP Computer Science Principles
overview: AP Computer Science Principles is a broad introduction to computing organized around five big ideas: creative development, data, algorithms and programming, computer systems and networks, and the impact of computing. The exam uses language-independent pseudocode (and block equivalents) and tests tracing algorithms, reasoning about data and abstraction, how the internet and parallel/distributed computing work, and the beneficial and harmful effects of computing innovations. A through-course Create performance task assesses program development, with written responses about that program on exam day.
examMode: Fully digital in the Bluebook app: multiple-choice and the written-response section are taken in Bluebook; the Create performance task's program, video, and Personalized Project Reference are submitted beforehand.

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Includes a set of questions based on a short reading passage about a computing innovation and several questions where two answers must be selected. The exam reference sheet defines the pseudocode.

sections.name: Create performance task
sections.notes: Students submit program code, a video of the program running, and a Personalized Project Reference (screenshots of a list and a procedure) in advance; on exam day they answer written-response questions about their own program using the PPR.

skills.name: 1. Computational Solution Design
skills.description: Design and evaluate computational solutions for a purpose.

skills.name: 4. Code Analysis
skills.description: Evaluate and test algorithms and programs.

skills.name: 5. Computing Innovations
skills.description: Investigate computing innovations and their effects.

skills.name: 6. Responsible Computing
skills.description: Contribute to an inclusive, safe, collaborative, and ethical computing culture.

scoring.summary: The multiple-choice section is 70% and the Create performance task (including exam-day written responses) is 30% of the score, converted to 1–5 using cut points set each year.

frqTypes.name: Create Written Response
frqTypes.howScored: Exam-day questions ask you to explain parts of your own program shown in your Personalized Project Reference: how a procedure's parameter changes its behavior, how a list manages complexity, what a selection or iteration statement does, and how you would test or modify the code. Points require responses specific to your code, not generic definitions.

strategy: Memorize the reference-sheet pseudocode: lists are 1-indexed, ← assigns, REPEAT UNTIL checks before each iteration.
Trace pseudocode with a variable table, especially loops that modify lists.
For multiple-select questions, evaluate each option independently; exactly two are correct.
For data questions, decide what information the data can and can't reveal (metadata vs content, correlation vs causation).
Know the internet's layered protocols at a conceptual level: IP addresses, packets, routing, TCP, HTTP, DNS, fault tolerance.
For impact questions, separate beneficial from harmful effects and identify who is affected.
On written responses, reference your exact list, procedure, and parameter names from your PPR.
Use process of elimination on 'which can NOT be determined' questions.
pitfalls: Using 0-based indexing on AP pseudocode lists.
Thinking more bits always means faster processing (bits limit the range of representable values).
Treating symmetric and public-key encryption as the same.
Assuming a heuristic always finds the optimal solution.
Confusing an undecidable problem with an unreasonable-time problem.
Equating the internet with the World Wide Web.
Assuming correlation in data proves causation.
referenceSheet: The Exam Reference Sheet defines pseudocode: assignment a ← expression; DISPLAY(expression); INPUT(); arithmetic including a MOD b; RANDOM(a, b) inclusive; relational and Boolean operators (=, ≠, <, ≤, >, ≥, NOT, AND, OR); IF/ELSE; REPEAT n TIMES; REPEAT UNTIL(condition); list operations (aList ← [value1, value2, ...], aList[i] with 1-based indexes, INSERT(aList, i, value), APPEND(aList, value), REMOVE(aList, i), LENGTH(aList), FOR EACH item IN aList); PROCEDURE definitions with RETURN; and robot commands (MOVE_FORWARD(), ROTATE_LEFT(), ROTATE_RIGHT(), CAN_MOVE(direction)).
